title: Paul in Athens (Acts 17:16–34)
hook: he quotes their own poets: in him we live and move and have our being

segments.voice: Yesterday, purple cloth: Lydia the seller of purple, and the jailer, and two men singing in the stocks.

Where do you start with someone who sees the world differently, at a wedding or in a comment thread? Most of us start with where they're wrong. Paul is in Athens, the ancient world's city of ideas, alone, waiting for his friends. He walks the streets, deeply stirred: the city is full of statues and altars to many gods, and he's a Jew who worships one. He talks in the synagogue and the marketplace with anyone who'll listen, Stoic and Epicurean philosophers among them. Some call him a babbler. Others are curious. They take him to the Areopagus, the council's hill, and say: tell us this new thing.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU START?` → `A CITY OF IDEAS.` → `UP TO THE AREOPAGUS.`

segments.voice: Paul begins with a compliment: I see you're a very religious people. Walking around, he says, I found an altar inscribed, in the King James Bible: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD." He doesn't mock it; he starts from it. The one you honor without knowing is the one I proclaim: the God who made the world, who doesn't live in buildings made by hands, and isn't far from any of us. Then, unexpectedly for a traveling Jewish teacher, he quotes their own poets: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring." The second line is from the Greek poet Aratus, about three centuries earlier; the first is often credited to another, Epimenides, though scholars aren't sure. Either way, Paul stands on their hill and speaks their language. Then he reaches his center: a day of judgment, and a man raised from the dead. That's where the room splits: at the resurrection, some laugh. Others say, politely, we'll hear you again. A few believe, and Luke names two: Dionysius, a council member, and a woman, Damaris. Christians have long pointed to this speech as a way to talk across a gap: start with what's good and true in the other person's world, honor it, then say plainly what you believe. A line Paul borrowed from Greek poets has been prayed and sung by Christians ever since. In him we live.
screen: `TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` · `HE STARTS FROM WHAT THEY HAVE.` · `QUOTING THEIR OWN POETS.` · `SOME LAUGH. SOME STAY.` · then, large: `IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE.`

segments.voice: Picture someone with a view you don't share, a politics, a faith, a way of raising kids or spending money, and look for their altar to the unknown god: the thing they're reaching for that you can honor, like safety, fairness, freedom, or love for their family. Name it kindly; you don't have to agree, just find the good. If you pray, you can pray for them.
Unknown god. The inscription Paul found on an altar in Athens, which he used to introduce the God he'd come to tell them about.
Your line: in him we live. Tomorrow, two weeks of storm at sea. Day eighty-five.

howItsDone: Christians often point to Paul's speech on the Areopagus as a model for speaking respectfully with people of other views. The line 'in him we live, and move, and have our being' is widely used in prayers and hymns.

original.note: Greek: to an unknown god, the inscription Paul read on an altar in Athens.

trapdoor: what you thought: in him we live is a Bible verse.
what it means: it is, and Paul is quoting Greek poets to Greek listeners, starting from what's true in their world.
what a scholar hears: we are his offspring is from Aratus's Phaenomena; in him we live is often credited to Epimenides, but that attribution is uncertain.

sources.quoted: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.

notes: Acts 17:22: the KJV reads 'too superstitious'; the Greek deisidaimonesterous can mean 'very religious'. The script paraphrases as 'very religious' without quoting the KJV. Confirm.
Aratus (c. 315–240 BC) said to have lived 'about three centuries earlier'; confirm.
The attribution of 'in him we live' to Epimenides is traditional (via later Christian commentators) and uncertain; the script says so.
Areopagus: both the hill and the council that met there; the script says 'the hill where the city's council met'. Confirm.
Paul's being 'stirred' by the images is described from Acts 17:16 without judging Greek religion; confirm tone.

Audit (second sample): the unsourced superlative that the line 'became one of the most loved in the whole New Testament' is now the narrower claim that it has been used in Christian prayers and hymns ever since (which howItsDone already says).
